results.evidence: No statute numbers appear anywhere in the post. All legal rules described using general language ('constitutional violations,' 'speedy trial deadline,' 'diversion programs').

No individual attorney or legal-scholar names appear. The TLDR quote is attributed to 'a principle consistent across elite defense methodology,' not a named person. Bureau of Justice Statistics is a source agency, not an expert.

One statistic found: '25-30% of felony arrests do not result in conviction' — sourced in-line as '(Bureau of Justice Statistics — State Court Processing Statistics)' with bjs.gov reference. No unsourced statistics.

All procedural references use general language ('the speedy trial deadline,' 'many jurisdictions offer diversion programs,' 'in some jurisdictions, defense attorneys can present evidence to the grand jury'). No bare universal deadlines or filing requirements.
Only excepted terminology appears: 'Brady violation' (×2) and 'Miranda violation' (×1). No other case citations in 'X v. Y' format found.
No collateral-consequence claims found. Post discusses case outcomes (dismissal, conviction, sentencing) but never claims specific licensing, housing, firearm, voting, or employment consequences.

results.reason: Frontmatter has no question_count field; body contains approximately 11 attorney-directed questions with no declared count to validate against.
The primary statistic (25-30% of felony arrests) is sourced to Bureau of Justice Statistics; remaining content is process description and strategic analysis, not unsourced factual claims.
Action items use plain language ('Email these five questions to your attorney today,' 'Look up your case on your court's online portal right now') well within 10th grade level.
Zero instances of the flagged cliches (at the end of the day, tip of the iceberg, slippery slope, double-edged sword, game changer, wake-up call) found in the post.
Post maintains second person ('you,' 'your') consistently throughout; third-person references ('the prosecutor,' 'the victim') refer to other parties, not the reader.
Approximately 12-15% of sentences use passive voice ('can be dropped,' 'may be suppressed,' 'can be dismissed'), well under the 30% threshold.
At least 6 legal terms used without definition on first use: arraignment, Miranda violation, directed verdict, mistrial, discovery, probable cause, continuance, restitution.
Follows clear problem (intro) → context (who has power) → solution (7 reasons charges drop) → clarification (what doesn't work) → action (what you can do) → CTA (bottom line).
Multiple actionable CTAs: 11 attorney questions, link to Case Progress Score, 'email these five questions today,' links to related posts, and concrete do/don't checklists.
Action statements are direct and unhedged ('Ask your attorney,' 'Email these five questions,' 'Delete any social media posts'); hedging appears only in informational context.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs are concise, typically 1-3 sentences under 100 words.
Largest section (Reasons Charges Get Dropped) is approximately 39% of total word count, under the 50% threshold.
Every threat is paired with action within 2 sentences — e.g., 'apologies can be used as evidence of guilt' immediately followed by 'Don't apologize to anyone except your attorney.'
Opens with relatable question hook, builds with 7 evidence-based dismissal grounds, closes with 3 concrete action steps and a free tool CTA — strong arc throughout.

results.evidence: Post issues direct commands without attorney guidance: 'Delete any social media posts about your case right now. Set your accounts to private.' and 'Do not apologize to anyone about your case except your attorney. Do not post about it online. Do not contact the alleged victim.'

The 'What Does NOT Get Charges Dropped' section discusses sentencing impact and diversion eligibility without a proximate attorney redirect, and the 'Timeline' table section has no attorney redirect despite covering legal decision stages.
Post uses general framing throughout ('charges get dropped for specific legal reasons') and never renders judgment about the reader's specific case strength or likely outcome.
All motion references are framed as what the attorney should be doing ('What your attorney should be doing: Filing a motion to suppress'), not as actions the reader should take directly.
The post does not discuss immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, DACA, or green card implications, so no immigration-specific attorney redirect is required.
The post does not assert specific collateral consequences such as license loss, housing restrictions, firearm rights, or voting rights — it focuses exclusively on dismissal grounds.
No specific bail bond companies, law firms, public defenders, or legal service providers are named; all references use general categories like 'your attorney' and 'the prosecutor.'

The post avoids first-person plural recommendations; the closest is the disclaimer ('We are not attorneys and do not provide legal representation'), which is a disclosure, not a legal-action recommendation.

Multiple narrative vignettes are not labeled as hypothetical: 'You're standing in a hallway outside the courtroom,' 'You're sitting in your attorney's office and they say,' 'Your phone screen glows at 1 AM,' and 'You tell your attorney you're a good person' — all could be mistaken for describing the reader's actual situation.

Post consistently frames knowledge as empowering attorney communication — 'Ask your attorney,' 'your attorney's job is to make that math work in your favor,' 'give that timeline to your attorney' — never implying the reader can handle the matter alone.

Legal rules stated as universal certainties without jurisdiction qualifiers: 'Apologies are not a legal defense,' 'the victim doesn't press charges or drop charges,' and 'Being a first-time offender does not automatically lead to dismissal' — none include 'in most jurisdictions' or similar hedging within their sections.

'If you successfully complete the program... the charges are dropped or the case is dismissed' states a guaranteed outcome without qualifying that results vary by jurisdiction; similarly 'A grand jury that refuses to indict effectively kills the case' implies a certain outcome.

Legal strategies including motion to suppress, Brady violation challenges, witness credibility investigation, and prosecutorial discretion pressure are presented as general defense methodology without attribution to any named case, statute, legal scholar, or attorney.

All legal statements are internally consistent — the post maintains a coherent position on who holds charging power, what grounds support dismissal, and the distinction between charging and sentencing factors throughout.

The Case Progress Score is framed as a research and question-generating tool: '5 minutes to see what's been done, what's missing, and what questions to ask next' — not as a substitute for legal representation.

Opening hook is strong ('It's the first question every defendant asks'), but 4+ H2s are topical rather than action-oriented: 'Who Has the Power to Drop Charges?', 'Reasons Charges Actually Get Dropped', 'What Does NOT Get Charges Dropped', 'The Timeline' — none frame what the reader GETS.

Most legal terms defined inline (nolle prosequi, Brady violation, PTI), but 'motion to suppress' first appears without inline definition and 'directed verdict' in the timeline table is unexplained — 2 terms missing.

No concrete immediate-action block before the first H2. The TLDRBox 'Your Next Step' requires an attorney ('Ask your attorney…'). The opening paragraphs are pure setup with no 'do this right now' action a defendant can complete alone in under 5 minutes.

Every section leads with a default: push your attorney to file motions, check docket filings, explore diversion eligibility. No section presents 3+ options without a recommendation. 'The earlier the better' is stated as the clear default.
'Ask the right questions' presents 5 unranked questions and 'Don't make it worse' presents 5 unranked don'ts — both hit the 5+ unranked threshold with no 'start with these' priority markers.
Single-post audit — structural pattern is system-decoder-post (explains who holds power, what mechanisms exist, how the process works).

Every threat is paired with action within 2 sentences: '25-30% don't result in conviction' pairs with 'ask your attorney about dismissal grounds'; 'apology can be used as evidence of guilt' pairs with 'don't apologize to anyone except your attorney.'

Zero blame language throughout. Person is consistently separated from situation — 'charges don't get dropped because you're a good person' frames the system's logic, not the reader's character. No 'you should have' or 'you failed to' patterns anywhere.

Opening acknowledges the universal question but doesn't deeply name the fear. Closing paragraph ends with 'your chances of dismissal are close to zero' (threat) followed by a CTA ('Take the free Case Progress Score') — not an agency statement. Arc is mostly present but final beat is fear+CTA instead of competence.
Timeline table has 3 columns (Stage / Can Charges Be Dropped? / How?). 'Reasons Charges Actually Get Dropped' section spans 7 H3 subsections totaling well over 600 words before the next H2.
'The Timeline' and 'The Bottom Line' H2 sections have no bolded screenshot sentence at all. Additionally, some bolded sentences exceed 27 words (e.g., the court docket sentence runs ~30 words).

All 3 FAQ answers start with direct answers ('Yes', 'The prosecutor has almost exclusive power', 'Neither will get charges dropped on its own'), run 3-4 sentences each, and read naturally as standalone support-group replies.
